title: STEGASUS: A Four-Expert Computational Framework for Breast Cancer Lymph-Node Metastasis Detection Using Patch-Based Deep Learning, Spatial Graph Analysis, and Calibrated Logistic Stacking
abstract: Detecting small metastatic deposits in breast cancer lymph-node tissue remains challenging for computational pathology. This study developed STEGASUS, a four-expert framework integrating EfficientNetB0, MobileViT-XXS, ResNet50, and a Spatial Graph Expert through calibrated logistic stacking. PatchCamelyon patches were grouped into 216 training, 54 development, and 128 labeled test source-slide groups. Matched spatial controls, expert-removal analyses, and supplementary shared-feature CLAM, DTFD-MIL, and channel attention-based CAMIL comparisons examined performance. The frozen ensemble achieved 91.41% accuracy, 77.08% sensitivity, 100.00% specificity, and AUROC of 0.9945. Its Brier score of 0.0565 and log loss of 0.2072 were lower than those of the primary supplementary comparators, while Spatial Graph and DTFD-MIL achieved stronger threshold-specific detection. Adjusted primary average-precision tests did not establish an ensemble advantage. DTFD-MIL had the most stable AP across three seeds; CAMIL showed substantial variation. STEGASUS detected 17 of 27 internal micrometastasis groups and 20 of 21 macrometastasis groups. Frozen processing of 20 selected CAMELYON16 WSIs yielded 80.00% accuracy and 60.00% sensitivity. Supplementary evaluation covered 85,054 CAMELYON17-WILDS patches from 10 slides and nine patients; all slides appeared in the prior inventory, and all sampled bags were positive. These limitations prevented a claim of independent whole-slide validation. A public research website and local analysis host were implemented, with end-to-end upload verification and participant usability outcomes unestablished. Findings supported computational feasibility and lower sampled probability error while identifying micrometastasis detection and independent validation as priorities.

tables.title: Analytical roles of the three STEGASUS phases.
rows: Training: expert fitting. Development: stacking, calibration and thresholds.
Sampled evaluation of experts, spatial edges and ensemble variants.
Frozen experts, graph, stacker and threshold; no refitting.
20-slide feasibility evaluation, ensemble predictions, patch-score heatmaps and processing records.
Public research website and local WSI analysis workspace
Existing frozen inference pipeline; no application-driven model refitting.
Study presentation, upload and case-review implementation, and limited public-interface checks.

tables.title: Major computational risks and corresponding STEGASUS safeguards.
rows: Related patches or misaligned predictions can distort comparisons.
Preserve source-slide identity and patch-row correspondence; check partition IDs, coordinate validity and label alignment. Patient independence remains unverified.
An inferred label could bias the evaluation.
Exclude test_049 from labeled evaluation because an authoritative label was unavailable; do not infer its label from predictions.
Repeated inspection can produce optimistic comparisons.
Describe the sampled evaluation as exploratory. Keep fitted predictions and thresholds fixed during resampling; these controls do not undo prior test reuse.
Cropping can alter the central region associated with the supplied label.
Retain the complete 96 x 96 patch; use flips for training and architecture-specific normalization without evaluation augmentation.
Changing several components together can obscure their contributions.
Match graph-head initialization and training order within each seed; compare self-only adjacency separately from refitted expert-removal stackers.
Accuracy alone can conceal missed positive slides or unstable estimates.
Report sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, AUROC, AP and confusion counts together with uncertainty. State the limited development-positive count.
Ranking, probability quality and fixed-threshold detection can differ.
Use development calibration and thresholds; report Brier score and log loss alongside discrimination and detection. Scores are not validated clinical patient risks.
Sampled patches do not provide complete tissue coverage or verified tumor boundaries.
Separate sampled evaluation from whole-slide processing. Treat patch scores and attention as computational outputs; assess localization separately.
Results may not be reproducible or comparable across runs.
Retain configurations, prediction files, IDs, thresholds and training histories; report matched graph-head seeds and distinguish their uncertainty from full-model retraining.

figures.caption: Conceptual STEGASUS computational framework. Model development and sampled source-slide evaluation are followed by frozen whole-slide processing and the application component. The diagram distinguishes the purpose of each phase; it does not imply that the later phases independently validate the sampled classification results.

Detailed three-phase STEGASUS workflow. Phase I shows the implemented development and comparison procedures. Phase II identifies the 20-image whole-slide processing outputs, and Phase III identifies the application component. The implemented public website and local analysis host are described in Section 2.5; application checks and their limitations are reported separately from model performance.

Conceptual illustration of source-slide grouping. The left panel illustrates how patch-wise mixing can distribute patches from the same source slide across partitions. The right panel keeps each sampled source-slide bag within its assigned partition. The labeled boxes are schematic examples, not an additional dataset or a patient-level independence analysis.

Image and spatial representations in the four-expert STEGASUS framework. The image experts generate patch probabilities that are aggregated by the maximum within a source slide. The graph expert combines frozen 1,280-dimensional EfficientNetB0 features with original coordinates and attention pooling. The four aligned slide scores are then transformed, standardized, stacked, and calibrated.

Conceptual comparison of spatial and self-only adjacency. Spatial adjacency permits information exchange between nearby patches and retains self-loops. Self-only adjacency removes interpatch communication while retaining the graph-head architecture. The sketch is not an observed tissue map, and the number of drawn edges does not represent the implemented eight-neighbor graph.

Development-fold fitting, calibration, and threshold selection. Five outer stratified folds produced out-of-fold (OOF) development scores. Within each outer fitting partition, three inner folds separated classifier fitting from sigmoid calibration. Scaling was fitted within the corresponding fitting folds. The selected operating threshold was subsequently applied to the final ensemble's test scores.

Paired class-stratified bootstrap comparison. Positive and negative source-slide groups are resampled separately, and identical sampled indices are used for both models. Each replicate yields a metric difference. Percentile intervals summarize uncertainty conditional on the fitted predictions; they do not account for all training variation or correct prior test-informed development.

Individual-expert performance on 128 sampled source-slide groups. Panel A shows classification and ranking measures; its color scale spans 0.70-1.00, with darker cells indicating larger values. Panels B and C show Brier score and log loss on separate zero-based scales, where lower values are preferable; row order is shared. Labels retain the reported four-decimal estimates. These exploratory point estimates do not establish pairwise statistical differences.

Recorded training loss across five epochs. Image-expert losses are shown separately from the Spatial Graph loss because they summarize patch-level and slide-level objectives, respectively. Lines connect recorded epochs; no smoothing or validation-loss values are added. Decreasing training loss alone does not establish generalization or absence of overfitting.

Spatial and self-only graph performance across three matched training seeds (42, 123, and 2026). Points show means and horizontal whiskers show one standard deviation, not confidence intervals. Each panel uses its own displayed scale; the two numeric labels give spatial and self-only mean � standard deviation, respectively. Higher values are preferable except for Brier score and log loss. Variability describes graph-head training, not independent retraining of all image encoders.

Calibrated ensemble performance on 128 sampled source-slide groups. Points show estimates and horizontal whiskers show the reported 95% confidence intervals; labels give estimate [lower bound, upper bound]. Classification and ranking measures are separated from Brier score and log loss because metric direction and scale differ. Intervals retain the methods described in Section 2.6 and do not account for prior test-informed development.
Confusion matrices for the six principal configurations.
figures.note: Note. Each matrix uses 128 sampled source-slide groups and its development-selected threshold.

figures.caption: ROC, precision-recall, and calibration curves.
figures.note: Note. Panels show continuous-score behavior on the same test groups. Calibration uses five quantile bins; AP is reported separately from trapezoidal curve area.

figures.caption: Complete calibrated ensemble and leave-one-expert-out variants on the sampled source-slide groups. Panel A shows classification and ranking measures on a color scale spanning 0.70-1.00; panels B and C show Brier score and log loss on separate zero-based axes with shared row order. All point estimates are labeled to four decimal places. Each variant was refitted and used its own development-selected threshold. These comparisons describe complete prediction pipelines rather than the effect of removing a fixed coefficient.

Frozen ensemble scores for 20 selected CAMELYON16 whole-slide images, grouped by reference label. The dashed line marks the fixed operating threshold of 0.628536. Hatched bars identify the four false negatives (test_004, test_010, test_011, and test_013); all ten reference-negative slides were classified as negative. Scores are labeled to four decimal places and are not validated patient-risk probabilities. This selected cohort provides exploratory feasibility evidence.
Overview interface of the deployed STEGASUS research website, showing study navigation, the four-expert framework, selected performance indicators, and access to the slide workspace.

Primary comparison of the frozen STEGASUS baseline, Spatial Graph, and three adapted MIL heads on 128 sampled source-slide groups. Comparator seed 42 was primary; scores describe the implemented shared-feature protocol.

ROC, precision-recall, and five-bin calibration plots for the primary comparison. Ranking curves and fixed-threshold detection describe different aspects of performance. These curves do not establish patient-level independence.
Average precision across three seeds for each adapted MIL comparator. Whiskers show one sample standard deviation. The common encoder remained frozen.

Recorded MIL-head inference cost averaged across the three available seeds. Cached feature input excludes patch extraction and encoder computation; measurements do not describe complete WSI processing time.
Supplementary patch-level discrimination and classification at hospital 2. The fixed patch threshold was 0.5. Patch dependence and documented prior source exposure limit interpretation.
Example ResNet50 patch-score map at observed coordinates for WILDS patient_040_node_2. The image displays sampled patch scores and is not a verified lesion mask or an ensemble localization output.
